newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS - Unshackled ICI Australia eyes Asia.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Unshackled ICI Australia eyes Asia.

text.p: Chemical and plastics group ICI Australia Ltd (ICIA) reinforced its Asian growth aspiration on Monday after U.K. parent ICI Plc's successful float of its majority stake in the company.
"Progressively I trust investors will see a company that has become more geographically diversified with a particular focus on Asia," ICIA chief, Philip Weickhardt told a media briefing.
Weickhardt said ICIA had good opportunities to grow its Asian sales of explosives, water treatment chemicals and consumer items like specialised paints.
"We have unique strengths here where we will have opportunities," Weickhardt said.
"In terms of our growth into Asia, we are mindful of generating profits and returns. We are going to focus on areas we genuinely think we can earn superior returns," he said.
ICI Plc announced in May it would sell most of its 62.4 percent stake in ICIA to help fund its US$8 billion acquisition of Unilever's specialty chemical business.
The offer of 143 million ICIA shares closed oversubscribed on Friday at a fixed offer price of A$12.35 for institutions and A$11.95 for retail investors.
ICIA said its largest identifiable shareholder was now the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP) with a five percent stake.
Analysts said ICIA's Asian expansion opportunities were previously seen restricted by ICI Plc paint division's large investment in Asia.
There was also suspicion in the investment community that ICI Plc had not lent much support to ICIA's development initiatives, analysts said.
"I think it is fair to say the perception was ICI Plc was happy to see ICIA concentrate on its Australian business," a Melbourne-based analyst said.
ICIA negotiated 31 agreements with its former parent before the float which allow it to compete with ICI Plc in any market except explosives, refinished paints and can coating areas.
For its profitable explosives division, the company negotiated a wider area for its operations that included all of the Asia/Pacific region east of India.
ICIA's explosives business had sales of A$150 million in Asia in the year to September 30, 1996, the company supplying most of the world's largest miners in this region.
Last month, ICIA's board approved a A$15.6 million investment to establish a joint venture explosives plant in China.
Weickhardt said despite the company's promising future in Asia, ICIA's medium term earnings outlook remained strongly tied to the performance of the Australian economy.

"We are pleased with the level of demand in the (Australian) mining and agricultural areas but I'm still very concerned that we are not seeing sustained signs of a pick-up that we would hope to see in the manufacturing and building construction areas," he said.
ICI shares resumed trading at 12.00 p.m (0200 GMT) on the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX). The shares sold by ICI Plc commenced trading at A$12.49, a slight discount to the remaining ordinary stock.

Dealers said the discount of the former ICI Plc stock was due to an overhang of sellers looking for a fast profit. ICI ordinary shares closed nine cents weaker at A$12.61 while the defferred shares ended at A$12.58.
-- Melbourne Bureau 61-3 9286-1435
